title: How are you managing take profits and stop losses for your AI trading agents?
author: ogb-officials
selftext:
I've built multiple profitable AI trading agents, and I can show proof. But one thing I've learned is that exits and timing are just as important as the strategy itself.

A lot of people simply tell their agents to trade or build a strategy without defining take profits, stop losses, or trailing stops to protect profits. People are having unrealistic expectations for agentic trading

Sometimes, you need to work backwards when building a trading strategy. Instead of just telling your agent to find profitable trades, why not start with something like: "Let's build a strategy that has a 70% probability of hitting a 25% profit target." Allow the agents to explore multiple scenarios + regime filters to find this one edge first. 

Of course, that probability needs to be tested, not just assumed. Once you define proper risk management, you'll realize that some strategies shouldn't be delegated to AI agents, while others can improve significantly.

How are you guys' handling exits and risk management with your agents?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Working backwards from a target is a risky way to do it, because if you ask an agent for a setup with a 70% chance of a 25% gain, it will usually find one that fits the old data. I'd let the data decide the exits, then check that the win rate times the average win still beats the average loss after fees. Hard stops and loss limits should sit outside the agent, so it can't talk itself out of them. Cymetica's Backtest Labs lets you set fees and max positions and keep the last 30% aside as out-of-sample, which is a good place to check this.

replies.author: ogb-officials
replies.body: I disagree here. That's why you both backrest and forward test with paper. You need to let your agent experience what it means to trade live too. Agent needs structure and rules to follow, not just plain prompt. People are optimizing agents for too many things and that's why it fails.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Fair point, and I agree that rules and a forward test on paper matter a lot. My only worry was about picking the 70% and 25% target first, because the search can bend to fit it. If the agent works within fixed rules and you judge it on live paper results, that part is sound. Fewer things to optimize does seem to help too.
